back: The rigid outer shell of the Earth (crust plus the uppermost mantle), about 100 km thick on average; it is broken into plates that move over the asthenosphere.
Continental: thick (about 35 km), lighter (about 2.7 g/cm³), very old, not subducted. Oceanic: thin (5-10 km), denser (about 3.0 g/cm³), young (under about 200 million years), subducted.
New oceanic crust forms at a mid-ocean ridge and moves away on both sides; basalt is youngest at the axis and older with distance.
Rate = distance from the ridge ÷ age of the rock. 1 km per million years = 1 mm per year.
Jigsaw fit of the shelves, matching fossils (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris), matching rocks, past climates, palaeomagnetic stripes and the age of the ocean floor.
The force of a cold, dense subducting slab sinking into the mantle and pulling the plate behind it: usually judged the strongest driver of plate movement.
Gravity sliding of lithosphere down the slope away from the raised mid-ocean ridge, pushing the plate.
Divergent (constructive): move apart. Convergent (destructive): move together, with subduction. Collision: continent meets continent. Conservative (transform): slide past each other.

front: Where is Zimbabwe on the plate map?
back: In the interior of the African (Nubian) plate, on an ancient craton, far from plate boundaries, so earthquakes and volcanoes are rare.
